Replication Example

gxrepl copies a primary's records to a copy, which keeps its own B-tree and vector index object by object, rebuilds a folder on its own after a fault, and goes on.

What It Shows

Database replication with gxrepl (the administrator's guide), object by object:

  1. The primary writes records (a name, a day and a vector member) and keeps two indexes made from them in the same gxdJournal transaction: a B-tree of names and a vector index. Its journal's ship log carries each commit's pages and, with the object notes on, which records the commit added, changed and removed. The two indexes are left out of the ship log.
  2. gxrepl sends the commits to the copy over gxStream (mutual TLS). The copy never receives the indexes: it keeps its own, updated object by object from the records each commit changed (derived_apply = incremental), with the example's extractor example_records (replication_records.h). The extractor turns a record into its B-tree key and its vector. It is built into the copy's gxrepl (replication_gxrepl), the way an application builds its own.
  3. When the copy cannot be sure of an index (a damaged stamp, a gap in the log, an extractor error), gxrepl says "rebuild needed", rebuilds that one folder in full on its own (replication rebuild, the set's derived_rebuild), and goes back to object by object. A full rebuild on every change is still a set's own choice: derived_apply = rebuild.
  4. replication digest prints what each index holds, whatever its layout: the B-tree's keys in order and the vector index's live nodes. The primary and the copy print the same.

Running It

The walkthrough runs it all on throwaway folders of this machine (127.0.0.1), with throwaway certificates made by the openssl command (POSIX only):

examples/oodb/replication_walkthrough.sh BUILD/examples

It starts the copy (replication_gxrepl serve), the primary's replicator (replication_gxrepl run) and the writer (replication write), then: (1) waits for the copy to follow object by object; (2) damages the copy's vector index stamp, and shows gxrepl's "rebuild needed" line, the folder rebuild and the way back to object by object; (3) compares the digests on both nodes. It exits with 0 when every check passes. KEEP=1 keeps its work folder, with both configs and both logs.

Sample Output

== 1. The copy follows object by object
derived state: 66 ok incremental lsn 34
  set records: derived_apply incremental, extractor example_records, source data.gxd ...
== 2. A simulated fault: the copy's vectors.vix.stamp damaged
  log: ... set records: .: derived indexes: rebuild needed: vectors.vix has a damaged stamp
  log: ... set records: .: derived indexes rebuilt for generation 142 (busy: never quiet)
derived state: 158 ok incremental lsn 80
== 3. The writer finishes; both nodes hold the same indexes
primary:
  by_name.btx btree 3f0c... 2314 keys
  vectors.vix logical 9a51... 2314 nodes
copy:
  by_name.btx btree 3f0c... 2314 keys
  vectors.vix logical 9a51... 2314 nodes
OK: object by object, one automatic folder rebuild after the fault, and the same indexes on both nodes

(The numbers differ from run to run; the two digests always agree.)

Files

examples/oodb/replication.cpp (the writer, the rebuild and the digest), replication_records.h (the record, the key and the extractor), replication_gxrepl.cpp (the example's gxrepl: gxrepl's own source built with GXREPL_EXTRA_EXTRACTORS, plus this file registering the extractor) and replication_walkthrough.sh, built by examples/CMakeLists.txt and run by tests/run_tests.sh.
